name: Sangameswarar Temple, Bhavani
deity: Shiva as Sangameswarar, with the goddess Vedanayaki (Vedambikai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kongu country at a river confluence, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); medieval and later additions
dynasty: Medieval Tamil patrons (Kongu, Vijayanagara and later)
summary: Sangameswarar is the Shiva temple of the Kooduthurai at Bhavani, the Thirunana of the Tevaram, where the Kaveri and the Bhavani meet a hidden third stream in the Dakshina Triveni, and where Sambandar's hymn is sung to the Lord of the confluence.

sections.history: In the western Kongu country, the Bhavani river runs into the Kaveri at a place known as Kooduthurai, the meeting-ford. The Tevaram hymns call the town Thirunana, and the verses of the child-saint Sambandar make the temple a Paadal Petra Sthalam; centuries later Arunagirinathar also praised it in his Tiruppugazh. Tradition and inscriptions show the shrine tended by successive rulers of the region, and a local account credits a Vijayanagara-era chieftain with raising its compound wall. Local memory also holds a colonial-era tale: a British collector is said to have offered a gold plate to the goddess in 1804, though the account is not firmly documented. What is certain is the long, unbroken worship at a spot that pilgrims have gathered at since the age of the hymns.
sections.architecture: The temple stands beside the river at the confluence, a walled Dravidian complex whose compound wall is attributed locally to a Vijayanagara-era chieftain. The sanctum of Sangameswarar holds the self-manifested linga, and the goddess Vedanayaki is honoured in her own shrine. Within the enclosure there is also a separate shrine of Vishnu with his consort Soundaravalli, so that Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion share one sacred precinct. Worship is offered in six services through the day. The meeting of the waters beside the walls is the temple's great setting, and the river bank next to it is where devotees go down to bathe.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of Kubera, lord of wealth, who came here on a pilgrimage among Shiva's shrines. At the confluence he saw natural enemies, tiger and deer, cow, elephant and snake, drinking side by side without fear, and a heavenly voice bade him worship Shiva in that place. In another telling, when Kubera tried to lift the linga a jet of water burst forth and flowed as a hidden river, the Amudha, to join the Bhavani and the Kaveri. This is the third stream of the Triveni, called Agaya Gangai in some accounts and the Saraswati in others. Sages such as Vishvamitra and Parasara are also remembered as worshippers, and a folk tradition speaks of a secret passage linking this shrine to Chidambaram.
sections.festivals: The annual Brahmotsavam is held in the Tamil month of Chithirai (April to May), when the deities are taken out in procession. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Because the river runs from north to south at this point, the confluence is held especially holy for rites in memory of ancestors, and new-moon days draw many families to its bank. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Begin at the water, where the rivers meet, and let the stillness of the confluence set the pace of your visit. Then enter the temple and come before Sangameswarar, before turning to the goddess Vedanayaki in her own shrine, and pause at the shrine of Vishnu, a rare companionship of the two traditions. Many pilgrims come to offer prayers for their departed, and the place holds the quiet seriousness of such rites. The town is busy, yet by the river and within the walls there is a sense of an old and sheltering sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to around midday and again from late afternoon into the evening (some listings give roughly 6 am to 12:30 pm and 4 pm to 9 pm); listings conflict, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Bhavani lies about 15 km from Erode, whose junction is the nearest major railway station. The temple is roughly 1 km from the Bhavani bus stand, with buses from Erode, Salem, Tiruppur and Coimbatore. Coimbatore, with the region's airport, is around 95 to 105 km away.
